Introduction

About two years ago I posted an article, What books and textbooks do acousticians use? It began as an answer to a question I had asked and answered myself on Zhihu, and a number of fellow acousticians answered it there too. A few days ago I saw an article in Acoustics Today by the American professor Steven Garrett, One-Hundred Years of English-Language Acoustics Textbooks, which traces the history of acoustics textbooks in the United States over the past century. I found it fascinating, and in this post I’d like to share some of it with you.

Lord Rayleigh

Over the past 85 years, two textbooks have dominated in the United States: Morse’s Vibration and Sound (1948) and Kinsler and Frey’s Fundamentals of Acoustics (1962). But if we go right back to the beginning, it all starts with the Nobel laureate Lord Rayleigh’s The Theory of Sound, published in 1877 (and, I would add, with that other founding father, Helmholtz). Rayleigh wrote the first volume while recovering from rheumatic fever, and it is mainly concerned with general theorems for vibrating systems and their mathematical description. Because he was on a houseboat on the Nile at the time, it has very few references. Excuse me?! Only a giant could get away with that; today he couldn’t even get it into a journal. It reminds me of a LinkedIn post I saw the other day from someone complaining that their paper had been revised again and again and still couldn’t get past the reviewers -_-

But I digress. By the time Rayleigh wrote the second volume he was back to normal life, so it has plenty of references, especially to published experimental results. Its main subject is sound in fluids.

Rayleigh wrote the book from an experimenter’s point of view, a perspective that later textbooks did not carry on. As early as 1868 he had built his own laboratory, setting a precedent for university laboratories in Britain. When he succeeded Maxwell in 1879 as the second Cavendish Professor, the university allocated £1,500 (equivalent to US$3 million today) for laboratory teaching, acoustics included.

Philip Morse

The first truly influential textbook of the post-Rayleigh era was the second edition of Philip Morse’s Vibration and Sound (1948), which also served as the template for Kinsler and Frey’s Fundamentals of Acoustics. The third edition got a new title, one that acousticians will know rather better: Theoretical Acoustics. In its day it was the textbook for physics and communications engineering at MIT, where Morse taught the course himself, and every chapter ends with exercises. The book demands a solid grounding in mathematics; when I was working through the material on moving sources, I found it heavy going.

When the book was reissued in 1981, Morse wrote in the preface: “This book is no longer as popular as it was in the 1960 edition.”

Kinsler and Frey

The reason Morse’s book lost some of its popularity was these two authors’ Fundamentals of Acoustics. Amusingly, when the first edition came out in 1950, the editor of JASA (The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America) sent it to Morse, then regarded as the father of acoustics textbooks, for review. Morse declined, saying, in effect, that it would hardly be proper for him to review his own book.

In fact, most of the content of Fundamentals of Acoustics had been carried over from the second edition of Vibration and Sound, and several end-of-chapter problems were copied outright. So it seems today’s trick of renaming the variables and publishing the same paper twice has a citable precedent… The second edition made some changes, such as switching from centimeter–gram–second (CGS) units to meter–kilogram–second (MKS) units. Some variable names changed too: frequency became f, for instance, and vectors and complex variables were set in bold. It also added applications such as loudspeakers, microphones, speech, hearing and architectural acoustics, and I think these more applied chapters are very worthwhile. Later editions added underwater acoustics, nonlinear acoustics, shock waves and more.

For the six decades from 1960 to 2020, these four editions of Fundamentals of Acoustics dominated acoustics education in American science and engineering.

Steven Garrett

Garrett is the author of Understanding Acoustics: An Experimentalist’s View of Sound and Vibration. The book was originally to have been written by Rudnick and his son at UCLA, but Rudnick was already past seventy at the time, so it fell to his last doctoral student, Garrett, to write it. Rudnick’s research group held Rayleigh and his approximation methods in very high esteem.

As I understand it, people like Rayleigh and Rudnick approached physical problems from the physicist’s side, which is more down to earth than the mathematician’s. They used simpler approximations: as long as a method met the final requirements and came reasonably close to the exact solution, they were happy to solve the problem the quicker way. Today we would call that the engineering approach, or, as the Chinese saying goes, it doesn’t matter whether a cat is black or white, so long as it catches mice. Lord Rayleigh’s laboratory was clearly no idle hobby: it turned him into a practitioner. Someone once summed up Rayleigh’s spirit like this:

The dance between math and physics can be a thing of beauty but not if you force the feet of math to trample on the toes of physics

In his article Garrett gives a number of examples comparing his book with the earlier textbooks. I haven’t read Understanding Acoustics, and of the earlier books I’ve only read a little of Morse’s, so I’m in no position to judge.

Garrett concludes that Fundamentals of Acoustics is like Listerine mouthwash: nobody likes the taste, but you still use it twice a day. He does not deny, though, that Morse’s book and Kinsler and Frey’s led a great many people into acoustics. From the point of view of those of us who came later, Garrett and the other giants who have written textbooks deserve just as much credit.

For specific textbook recommendations, see my earlier article What books and textbooks do acousticians use?, which includes textbooks recommended by me and by TransLoss, another top answerer on acoustics on Zhihu, in both Chinese and English. The 17 people who answered the Zhihu question also made recommendations that, I think, cover most areas of acoustics. If you’re interested, have a look on Zhihu:
